lines: {target}? Green stalks can hide quick trouble.
The next person heading toward Bamboo Jungle needs your warning. Keep a path cut behind you.
Bamboo crowds the eye and the feet.
I'll remember Bamboo Jungle as a green wall that rustles like whispers.
Before things went wrong at the bamboo jungle, what warning did everyone miss?
The path back matters more than the path in. What did you use to find it?
What sort of footing gave you the most trouble near the bamboo jungle?
Could you see the way home once rain caught under the canopy began?
What did you rely on for drinking water near the bamboo jungle?
The dock will feel wonderfully ordinary after hearing that story.
What food would you carry twice as much of if you returned?
I would check every knot after that journey. What needs mending now?
Which place did you choose for camp, and what made you trust it?
Tell me you had steady company on that road.
Did the sounds around you make the danger seem closer than it was?
How much luck was left by the time you got clear?
How long did it take before the village felt close again?
What do people misunderstand most when they talk about the bamboo jungle?
Some journeys stay in the hands after the road ends. Is this one of them?
Would you guide another traveler there, or only warn them away?
{target}? Leaves crowd close enough to hide anything.
Make sure travelers know this before visiting Jungle. Cut a path and remember which vines you passed.
The green is loud even when nothing moves.
I'll remember Jungle as a hot forest that keeps secrets well.
At the jungle, which risk looked small until you were standing beside it?
A tired traveler can mistake any path for home. How did you avoid that near the jungle?
Did anyone fall when roots, leaf litter, and hidden holes turned worse?
How long could you travel once rain caught under the canopy set in?
I hope you filled every bottle before the jungle. Did you?
That trip makes a day in my little boat sound gentle.
Did you pack enough to share, or only enough to survive the trip?
Did wet, heat, or grit damage anything you depended on?
I hope your shelter had one good wall and no surprises.
Which traveler surprised you by staying calm near the jungle?
Could you smell the jungle before it came into view?
What looked harmless near the jungle until it began moving?
How many days passed before your legs forgave the journey?
Which mistake would you refuse to repeat near the jungle?
You came back changed, though perhaps only you can name how.
Do you think the place would feel different on a second visit?
{target}? Mud holds boots longer than plans.
Your best advice for Mangrove Swamp sounds simple. Step on roots and keep slime in mind.
Thick roots make every hurry foolish.
I'll remember Mangrove Swamp as muddy water with a grip on your ankles.
The first bad moment at the mangrove swamp must have changed the whole trip. What happened?
By the time you left the mangrove swamp, did you know the way or merely know what to avoid?
A person watches enemies and forgets the ground. Did the mangrove swamp punish that?
Did rain upstream follow you on the return trip?
How carefully did you ration water on the way to the mangrove swamp?
I would rather mend nets in rain than face deep channels and things under the surface.
Did something dry enough to eat last until you were safely headed home?
What did you leave behind because carrying it home was not worth the risk?
Shelter found after dark rarely feels as safe as it looks. How was yours?
A good companion notices fear without making a speech about it. Who noticed yours?
When water moving through reeds changed, did you know why?
How near did the trouble come before anyone noticed it?
The return is where small injuries begin to matter. Who needed help?
Which lesson from that place belongs in every travel pack?
There is a part of that story you keep circling. You can leave it alone if you want.
If the choice were yours tomorrow, would you stay home?
{target}? Thin jungle still keeps thick surprises.
I would tell anyone planning a trip to Sparse Jungle one thing. Don't trust open patches too quickly.
Vines and shadows take turns hiding things.
I will remember Sparse Jungle as green country pretending to be easier than it is.
How quickly did trouble find you around the sparse jungle?
Did the route home feel easier to recognize after everything you had seen?
Was the ground at the sparse jungle harder on your legs or on your nerves?
Was there a safe place to wait out rain caught under the canopy?
The road home feels different when the water is gone. How close did you come?
Give me rough water over movement beyond the trees any day.
How many meals did the journey take beyond what you expected?
Of everything you packed, what earned its place?
How many people shared the safest resting place near the sparse jungle?
Someone must have kept you moving when home felt far away. Who was it?
Did the silence there feel peaceful, or did it feel watched?
When trouble reached the group, who spotted the safest opening?
What part of the return from the sparse jungle felt longest?
What rule kept you alive once the original plan failed?
Thank you for trusting me with the part that was hardest to say.
Was one journey to the sparse jungle enough for a lifetime?
{target}? Mud and water both remember footsteps.
People setting out for Swamp should remember this. Watch slimes, witches, and the slow ground.
Fog makes close things feel far.
I'll remember Swamp as wet land that grabs at ankles and plans.
Tell me when the swamp stopped feeling like an adventure and started feeling dangerous.
On the way toward the swamp, where did the route become difficult to read?
Could you move quickly over mud, roots, and flooded ground, or did caution win?
At the swamp, what sign told you the conditions were about to worsen?
Could you refill near the swamp, or only ration what you carried?
There are days I complain about the lake. Today will not be one of them.
A hungry traveler makes quick mistakes. Did your food hold out?
A spare tool is dead weight until the first one fails. Which spare saved you?
How did you locate ground above the flood line when everyone needed rest?
Who remembered the plan when trouble scattered everyone?
Were there moments at the swamp when hearing less felt worse?
Were you able to wait for danger to move, or did it force your hand?
Was the path home kinder than the one that took you out?
If you could change one choice from that trip, which would it be?
I can hear how tired you were, even now.
Tell that story by the fire sometime. Others need the honest version.
